item.title: Blue-light labeling uncovers unexpected protein partners of folded DNA structures
item.description: DNA can be more than just a double helix. When four strands are folded into a compact bundle, they form a G-quadruplex (G4). These bundles form in guanine-rich regions across the genome, including telomeres at the ends of chromosomes and the control regions of genes, where the proteins that dock onto them help decide which genes are switched on. G4 does not act the same way everywhere. What it does depends on where it forms and which proteins bind to it. This is why understanding the interactions surrounding G4 is so important. Fuente: Phys.org.

Her findings show that relaxation occurs where tranquility, nature, safety and the presence of other people come together. By gathering input directly from older adults, she provides designers of public spaces with valuable insights into the needs of older residents. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heavy fermions emerge at an atomic-layer interface, unlocking new ways to design quantum materials
item.description: A research team led by the University of Osaka has directly observed, for the first time, an unusual heavy-fermion state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. Such states are closely linked to exotic quantum phenomena, including unconventional superconductivity, and the finding opens new possibilities for designing quantum materials through their interfaces. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Popular TikTok docs have big influence on Gen Z followers, new research finds
item.description: Young adults following physicians on TikTok consider them more accessible, credible and altruistic than their own doctors, even when the physician-influencers are selling products. Moreover, the followers haven't actually confirmed the influencers' medical credentials. Those are the main findings of a new study from Virginia Commonwealth University, co-authored by Suzanne Makarem, Ph.D., and published in the Journal of Consumer Affairs. Fuente: Phys.org.
